questions.question: Which Delhi sultan was known for his "Market Reforms"?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Alauddin Khalji**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Alauddin Khalji**, the second ruler of the **Khalji dynasty**, implemented significant reforms in the market system during his reign (1296–1316 AD) in the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• He introduced strict control over **prices of goods**, including essential commodities like grains, cloth, and horses, to avoid inflation and ensure affordability for common people.
 
• Alauddin Khalji's market reforms were aimed at curbing black marketing, hoarding, and exploitation by merchants and traders. He established a system of fixed prices and ensured their enforcement by appointing **officials known as market controllers**.
 
• He set up separate markets for different commodities, such as **"grain market" (mandi), cloth market, and livestock market**, which were closely monitored by his administration.
 
• To ensure fair trade practices and prevent corruption, Alauddin Khalji employed spies (**"barids"**) to keep an eye on merchants and monitor market activities. Severe punishments were imposed on those who violated the rules.
 
• These reforms were crucial to maintaining economic stability during his reign and reflected his administrative foresight and commitment to welfare.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Firoz Shah Tughlaq:**

 
 
• Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351–1388 AD), a ruler of the Tughlaq dynasty, is known for his contributions to **infrastructure development**, including canals, roads, and buildings.
 
• He introduced several welfare measures, such as the construction of hospitals and colleges, but did not implement significant market reforms.
 
 
 
• **Balban:**
 
 
• Balban (1266–1287 AD), a ruler of the Slave dynasty, focused on strengthening the central authority and military system. He introduced the **"Theory of Kingship"** but did not focus on market control or economic reforms.
 
• His reign was marked by efforts to curb the power of nobles and maintain law and order.
 
 
 
• **Iltutmish:**
 
 
• Iltutmish (1211–1236 AD), another ruler of the Slave dynasty, is best known for consolidating the Delhi Sultanate and introducing the **silver coinage system (Tanka)**.
 
• Although he made significant contributions to administrative and financial reforms, he did not implement market reforms like Alauddin Khalji.
 
 
 
• **Market Reforms under Alauddin Khalji:**
 
 
• Alauddin Khalji's market reforms were primarily driven by his military campaigns, which required the availability of affordable supplies for his armies.
 
• These reforms were an early example of state intervention in the economy to regulate trade and ensure social welfare.
 
• He successfully maintained price stability and prevented economic exploitation during his reign.
 
• The reforms showcased his administrative capabilities and highlighted the importance of a regulated economy in medieval India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Spies (Barids):** Alauddin Khalji extensively used spies to monitor market activities, ensuring strict implementation of his policies.
 
• **Price Control:** Fixed prices for all commodities were enforced, and violations were met with severe penalties.
 
• **Separate Markets:** Dedicated markets for grains, cloth, and other goods ensured better organization and regulation.
 
• **Economic Stability:** The reforms were crucial in maintaining affordability for common people and supporting his military campaigns.
 
• **Legacy:** Alauddin Khalji's market reforms are considered a landmark in the economic history of the Delhi Sultanate, showcasing the role of state intervention in medieval governance.

questions.question: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution is borrowed from Canada?

options.text: Advisory Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Advisory Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Advisory Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court**: This feature was borrowed from the **Canadian Constitution**. Under Article 143 of the Indian Constitution, the President of India can seek the opinion of the Supreme Court on questions of law or matters of public importance. This advisory role strengthens the judiciary's role in governance. 
• The **Canadian model of federalism** also influenced the Indian Constitution in other ways, such as the division of powers between the Union and States. 
• The advisory jurisdiction provides a mechanism for resolving legal uncertainties, ensuring clarity on constitutional or legal matters. This is a hallmark of the federal structure influenced by Canada. 
• None of the other options listed (Rule of Law, Impeachment of the President, Fundamental Duties) were borrowed from Canada. These features have their origins in other sources like the British Constitution, U.S. Constitution, or Soviet principles. 
• This distinctive feature in India ensures the Supreme Court’s role in offering legal counsel to the executive, promoting democratic accountability and rule of law. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Advisory Jurisdiction in Canada:** 
• The Canadian Supreme Court has a similar advisory jurisdiction, where the government can refer legal or constitutional questions to the court for its opinion. 
• This feature was adapted in India to ensure a consultative relationship between the judiciary and the executive. 
• **Article 143 of the Indian Constitution:** 
• This article empowers the President of India to refer questions of law or public importance to the Supreme Court. 
• The opinion provided by the Supreme Court under this article is advisory and not binding on the President. 
• Example: Presidential references like the **Keshav Singh case** or the **Babri Masjid demolition** are significant applications of this provision. 
• **Other Features Borrowed from Canada:** 
• **Federal system with a strong Centre:** The Indian Constitution follows a federal structure with a tilt towards central authority, inspired by Canada. 
• **Residuary Powers:** In India, the residuary powers (those not mentioned in the Union or State List) are vested with the Centre, similar to the Canadian model. 
• **Origins of Other Options:** 
• **Rule of Law:** Borrowed from the British Constitution, it signifies equality before the law and supremacy of law. 
• **Impeachment of the President:** Inspired by the U.S. Constitution, this process ensures checks and balances in a democracy. 
• **Fundamental Duties:** These were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, and were inspired by the Soviet Constitution. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Federal Features of Indian Constitution:** 
• India’s Constitution is federal in structure but unitary in spirit, influenced by the Canadian model. 
• Examples include division of powers, independent judiciary, and dual government system. 
• However, India has unique features like a single citizenship and flexibility in amending the Constitution, differentiating it from traditional federal states. 
• **Presidential Reference:** 
• One of the notable cases under Article 143 was the **Keshavananda Bharati case**, where basic structure doctrine was established. 
• Another example is the reference on the **Ayodhya land dispute** (2019).

questions.question: Which of the following is not covered under Article 25 of the Indian Constitution?

options.text: Right to profess and practice religion

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Right to religious conversion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 25** of the **Indian Constitution** guarantees the freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion to all citizens of India.
 
• The scope of Article 25 includes:
 
 
• **Freedom of conscience:** Every individual has the right to hold and express their personal religious beliefs.
 
• **Right to profess:** Individuals can openly declare and follow their chosen religion.
 
• **Right to practice:** Citizens are free to engage in religious rituals, customs, and ceremonies.
 
• **Right to propagate:** Citizens have the right to spread or communicate their religious beliefs to others.
 
 
 
• However, the **right to religious conversion** is not explicitly mentioned or protected under Article 25. Conversion through force, fraud, or inducement is not permissible under Indian law, as it violates public order and individual rights.
 
• While Article 25 protects individual freedoms, it is subject to reasonable restrictions related to **public order, morality, and health**, as well as the rights of other citizens.
 
• The term "propagate" does not imply a fundamental right to convert others through coercion or other unlawful means, as clarified by the judiciary in various judgments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Provisions under Article 25:**

 
 
• **Freedom of Conscience:** This allows individuals to hold their personal religious beliefs without interference from the state or others.
 
• **Right to Propagate:** This includes the right to spread religious beliefs but does not extend to forced conversion.
 
• **Reasonable Restrictions:** The state can impose restrictions to maintain public order, morality, and health, ensuring that religious practices do not infringe on others' rights.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Interpretation:**
 
 
• In the **Rev. Stainislaus vs. State of Madhya Pradesh (1977)** case, the Supreme Court ruled that the right to propagate does not include the right to convert others forcibly.
 
• The court upheld anti-conversion laws in several states, emphasizing that forced conversions disrupt public order.
 
 
 
• **Anti-Conversion Laws in India:**
 
 
• Several states, including **Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, and Odisha**, have enacted laws to regulate religious conversions.
 
• These laws aim to prevent conversions through **force, fraud, or inducement** while respecting individual freedoms.
 
 
 
• **Other Related Articles:**
 
 
• **Article 26:** Grants the right to manage religious affairs to religious denominations.
 
• **Article 27:** Prohibits the use of public funds for promoting or maintaining any religion.
 
• **Article 28:** Restricts religious instruction in educational institutions maintained by the state.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Reasonable Restrictions:** The state can regulate or restrict religious practices if they conflict with public order, morality, or health.
 
• **Secularism in India:** The Indian Constitution follows the principle of secularism, ensuring equal treatment of all religions without favoring or discriminating against any particular faith.
 
• **Religious Freedom Worldwide:** Many countries adopt different approaches to religious freedom. For example:
 
 
• The **First Amendment of the US Constitution** protects freedom of religion, including the right to practice and propagate one's faith.
 
• In contrast, countries like **France** emphasize strict secularism, restricting overt religious expressions in public spaces.

questions.question: The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank is headquartered in ________.
questions.solution: The correct answer is __**Beijing**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** • The **Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB)** is an international financial institution that focuses on financing infrastructure projects across Asia and beyond. • It was formally established in **December 2015**, and began operations in **January 2016**. • The headquarters of AIIB is located in **Beijing, China**, which reflects China's role as the leading initiator and largest shareholder in the bank. • AIIB aims to enhance economic development and regional cooperation by providing loans for infrastructure projects such as transportation, energy, water systems, and urban development. • It currently has **106 approved members** from across the globe, including major economies like India, Germany, and the UK.

questions.question: Agreement on cooperation in the peaceful uses of Nuclear energy was signed in ______ between India and Japan.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2016**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Agreement on Cooperation in the Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy** was signed between **India and Japan** on **11 November 2016**. 
• This agreement marked a significant milestone in bilateral relations between **India and Japan**, emphasizing their cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear energy. 
• The agreement allows Japan to supply nuclear reactors, fuel, and technology to India, which is not a signatory to the **Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT)**. This highlights Japan's recognition of India's commitment to peaceful nuclear energy uses. 
• India committed to adhering to stringent **International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)** safeguards to ensure that the nuclear materials and technology are used exclusively for peaceful purposes. 
• The agreement enables India to access advanced nuclear technologies from Japan, which is known for its expertise in the field, thereby supporting India's growing energy demands and climate change mitigation efforts. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **India's Nuclear Energy Program:** 
• India has ambitious plans for nuclear energy to meet its growing **energy demands** and reduce reliance on fossil fuels. 
• The country operates several nuclear reactors and has plans to expand its nuclear power capacity in the coming decades. 
• India is a signatory to the **Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreements** with multiple countries, including the USA, Russia, France, and Canada. 
• **Japan's Role in Nuclear Technology:** 
• Japan is renowned for its **advanced nuclear technology** and expertise in nuclear power generation. 
• Japan's nuclear industry has been pivotal in developing safe and efficient nuclear reactor designs, emphasizing safety standards post-Fukushima disaster. 
• Japan's cooperation with India reflects its trust in India's commitment to using nuclear energy responsibly. 
• **International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA):** 
• The IAEA is an international organization that promotes the peaceful use of nuclear energy and prevents its misuse for military purposes. 
• India has a longstanding association with the IAEA and has implemented its safeguards in civilian nuclear facilities. 
• Through its adherence to IAEA guidelines, India demonstrates its commitment to responsible nuclear energy usage. 
• **Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT):** 
• The NPT aims to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons and promote peaceful use of nuclear energy. 
• India is not a signatory to the NPT but has been recognized internationally for its responsible nuclear energy policies. 
• The India-Japan agreement signifies Japan's acknowledgment of India's responsible nuclear energy practices, despite non-adherence to the NPT. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Energy Demand in India:** 
• India's energy demand is projected to double by **2040**, making nuclear energy an essential component of its energy mix. 
• The agreement with Japan facilitates the transfer of advanced technologies to support India's energy goals and reduce carbon emissions. 
• **Significance of Civil Nuclear Agreements:** 
• Such agreements enable India to access critical nuclear technology and fuel from advanced nuclear nations. 
• They foster international cooperation, ensuring the peaceful use of nuclear energy and adherence to global safety standards. 
• **Global Energy Transition:** 
• Countries worldwide are transitioning to cleaner energy sources, and nuclear power plays a vital role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. 
• India's collaboration with Japan aligns with global efforts to combat climate change through sustainable energy solutions. </ul

questions.question: Hariprasad Chaurasia is a celebrated classical musician known for playing which instrument?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Flute**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Hariprasad Chaurasia** is an internationally renowned Indian classical musician, celebrated for his exceptional skill and mastery over the **flute**. 
• He is credited with popularizing the **bansuri**, a traditional Indian bamboo flute, in the realm of Hindustani classical music. 
• Born on **1 July 1938**, in Allahabad (now Prayagraj), Hariprasad Chaurasia pursued his passion for music despite his father’s desire for him to become a wrestler. 
• He received training in classical vocal music under **Raja Ram** before dedicating himself to learning the flute under the guidance of **Pandit Bholanath Prasanna**. 
• Hariprasad Chaurasia has collaborated with several prominent artists globally and has composed music for films, showcasing the versatility of the flute across various genres. 
• He has been honored with numerous awards, including the prestigious **Padma Bhushan (1992)** and **Padma Vibhushan (2000)**, for his immense contribution to Indian classical music. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **The Flute in Indian Classical Music:** 
• The **bansuri** is a side-blown bamboo flute that holds a significant place in Indian classical music, with its roots tracing back to ancient mythology and scriptures. 
• It is often associated with Lord **Krishna**, who is depicted playing the bansuri, symbolizing love and divinity in Indian culture. 
• The bansuri produces a melodious and soothing sound, making it ideal for expressing the intricate nuances of **raagas** in Hindustani classical music. 
• **Other Classical Instruments in India:** 
• **Sitar:** Popularized globally by maestros like **Pandit Ravi Shankar**, the sitar is a stringed instrument known for its complex sound and resonance. 
• **Tabla:** A pair of hand-played drums, the tabla is essential in Indian classical and folk music, providing rhythmic accompaniment. 
• **Violin:** Though of Western origin, the violin has been adapted into Indian classical music and is widely used in both Hindustani and Carnatic traditions. 
• **Hariprasad Chaurasia’s Global Influence:** 
• He has worked with renowned international artists like **George Harrison** of The Beatles and composer **John McLaughlin**, blending Indian classical music with global genres. 
• Hariprasad Chaurasia co-founded the **Vrindavan Gurukul** in Mumbai and Bhubaneswar to train young musicians in the art of flute playing. 
• His collaborations extend to Indian cinema, where he has composed music for iconic films like **Silsila** and **Lamhe**, alongside Pandit Shivkumar Sharma as the duo Shiv-Hari. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Awards and Recognitions:** 
• Hariprasad Chaurasia has received international accolades, including the **Sangeet Natak Akademi Award** and the **Konark Samman**. 
• He was conferred with honorary doctorates from prestigious institutions for his contribution to music education and preservation of Indian classical traditions. 
• **Legacy:** 
• Hariprasad Chaurasia’s work has inspired countless musicians worldwide to take up the flute and explore Indian classical music. 
• His teachings and performances continue to bridge cultural and musical gaps, promoting harmony and understanding through the universal language of music. 
55:T

questions.question: Which ministry has launched "Deen Dayal SPARSH Yojana" in August 2024?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ministry of Communications**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **Deen Dayal SPARSH Yojana** (Scholarship for Promotion of Aptitude & Research in Stamps as a Hobby) was launched by the **Ministry of Communications** in August 2017, with the aim to promote philately as a hobby among school students.

• The scheme provides a **scholarship** to students of classes VI to IX who display a strong inclination towards philately, which is the study and collection of postage stamps.

• The scholarship is awarded to students who score **60% or more marks** in their previous final examination and pass a philately quiz and project conducted by the postal department.

• The scheme also aims to develop a **scientific temperament** and a spirit of inquiry among students through the hobby of philately.

• Under this scheme, **40 scholarships** are awarded per postal circle, and each scholarship carries a monetary award of **Rs. 6,000 annually** (Rs. 500 per month).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Philately**: 

• Philately refers to the **study and collection of postage stamps and postal history**.

• It is considered an important educational and historical hobby, helping students understand the culture, history, and heritage of their country and the world.

• Philately is often referred to as the “**king of hobbies**” due to its wide appeal and historical significance.

• **Ministry of Communications**:

• The **Ministry of Communications** is responsible for the functioning of **India Post**, which oversees postal services in the country.

• The ministry includes two key departments: **Department of Posts** and **Department of Telecommunications**.

• The **Department of Posts** manages initiatives like philately and other schemes aimed at leveraging postal services for education and awareness.

• **Criteria for Deen Dayal SPARSH Yojana**:

• The scheme is open to students of classes VI to IX in recognized schools across India.

• Participants are required to have their own philately deposit account and submit a project on a philately-related topic.

• Students must pass a **philately quiz** and a **philatelic project** evaluation conducted by the postal circle.

• **Promotion of Philately**:

• India Post organizes various philately exhibitions, workshops, and competitions to promote this hobby among school students.

• Philately clubs are also being established in schools to encourage participation in stamp collection and related activities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Other Initiatives by India Post:**

• India Post organizes **National Philatelic Exhibitions** to showcase rare and unique stamps.

• Special initiatives like **My Stamp** allow individuals to create personalized stamps with their own photographs.

• **India Post's Role in Education:**

• The postal department actively contributes to promoting **education and awareness** through schemes like Deen Dayal SPARSH Yojana.

• It also runs initiatives for financial literacy and digital inclusion in rural areas.

• **Global Importance of Philately:**

• Many countries use philately as a medium to promote tourism, culture, and history.

• International philatelic exhibitions are held worldwide, fostering cultural exchange and historical preservation.

5c

questions.question: Who publishes the Global Terrorism Index 2024?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Institute for Economics and Peace**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **Global Terrorism Index (GTI)** is published annually by the **Institute for Economics and Peace (IEP)**, a global think tank headquartered in **Sydney, Australia**.

• The index provides a **comprehensive summary of global trends in terrorism**, analyzing its impact across countries and regions.

• The GTI measures terrorism using various indicators such as **number of incidents, fatalities, injuries, and property damage**.

• It is based on data collected by the **Global Terrorism Database (GTD)**, maintained by the University of Maryland.

• The report offers insights into **patterns of terrorism**, its causes, and societal impacts, making it a crucial resource for policymakers, academics, and researchers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Institute for Economics and Peace (IEP):**

• The IEP is an independent, non-partisan think tank established in **2008** with the aim to develop metrics for peace and to promote a better understanding of the drivers of peace.

• The organization is known for publishing global indices such as the **Global Peace Index (GPI)** and the **Global Terrorism Index (GTI)**.

• Its headquarters is located in **Sydney, Australia**, and it has offices in New York, Brussels, and Mexico City.

• IEP works on research related to **peace and conflict studies, economic impact of violence, and strategies to improve societal resilience.**

• **Global Terrorism Database (GTD):**

• The GTD is a comprehensive database on terrorist incidents worldwide, maintained by the **National Consortium for the Study of Terrorism and Responses to Terrorism (START)** at the University of Maryland.

• It includes data on over **200,000 terrorist events** from 1970 to the present.

• The database is widely used by researchers, policymakers, and institutions for analyzing terrorism trends and impacts.

• **Key Features of the Global Terrorism Index:**

• It categorizes countries based on their levels of terrorist activity, ranging from **the most affected to least affected.**

• The index highlights regions most vulnerable to terrorism and identifies trends in **terrorist tactics, motives, and organizational behavior.**

• It also explores **underlying factors** contributing to terrorism, such as political instability, socioeconomic factors, and conflicts.

• **Uses of the Global Terrorism Index:**

• Policymakers use the index to formulate **counter-terrorism strategies** and allocate resources effectively.

• Academics and researchers employ GTI data for studies on **global security, peacebuilding, and conflict resolution.**

• The index also informs international organizations, such as the **United Nations**, for crafting global initiatives to combat terrorism.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **SIPRI:** The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute focuses on research related to **conflicts, armaments, and disarmament**, but does not publish the Global Terrorism Index.

• **United Nations:** While the UN addresses global terrorism issues, it does not release a specific index such as the GTI.

• **WHO:** The World Health Organization is primarily concerned with global health issues and does not engage in terrorism-related studies.
</ul

questions.question: Which organization publishes the Human Development Report?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**UNDP**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Human Development Report (HDR)** is published annually by the **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)**. It was first launched in **1990** as an independent report commissioned by the UNDP. 
• The report introduces the **Human Development Index (HDI)**, which is a composite measure of health, education, and income, designed to assess and rank countries' development levels beyond just economic factors. 
• The HDR aims to promote the concept of **“human development”**, emphasizing the importance of expanding people's choices and improving their well-being, rather than focusing solely on economic growth. 
• Each year, the report highlights a specific theme related to global development challenges, such as inequality, climate change, or poverty, providing in-depth analysis and policy recommendations. 
• The HDR is considered one of the most influential publications in the field of international development and is widely used by policymakers, researchers, and organizations globally. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP):** 
• The **UNDP** was established in **1965** and is headquartered in **New York City**, USA. It is the **United Nations' global development network**. 
• It focuses on areas such as **poverty reduction**, **sustainable development**, **democratic governance**, and **climate and disaster resilience**. 
• The UNDP operates in **170 countries and territories**, working with governments and local communities to address development challenges. 
• The organization is also responsible for managing the **UN Volunteers programme** and the **United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF)**. 
• **Human Development Index (HDI):** 
• The HDI is a composite index that measures a country's average achievements in three basic aspects of human development: 
• **Health:** Measured by life expectancy at birth. 
• **Education:** Measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling. 
• **Standard of Living:** Measured by Gross National Income (GNI) per capita (adjusted for purchasing power parity). 
• The HDI ranks countries on a scale from **0 to 1**, with higher scores indicating higher levels of development. 
• The HDI is a key tool for comparing development levels across countries and identifying areas for improvement. 
• **Other Organizations in the Options:** 
• **IMF (International Monetary Fund):** The IMF focuses on global monetary cooperation and financial stability but does not publish the HDR. 
• **World Bank:** The World Bank emphasizes financial and technical assistance for development projects but does not produce the HDR. 
• **World Economic Forum (WEF):** The WEF is known for its Global Competitiveness Report and other economic studies, not the HDR. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• The HDR's overarching goal is to advocate for policies that prioritize **human well-being** over mere economic growth. 
• It has introduced several supplementary indices, such as the **Gender Inequality Index (GII)** and the **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)**, to provide a more nuanced understanding of development. 
• The HDR contributes to global discussions on sustainable development, helping shape the **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)** agenda adopted by the United Nations in 2015. 
• Notable contributors to the first HDR in 1990 included economists **Amartya Sen** and **Mahbub ul Haq**, who were instrumental in shaping the human development approach. 
6a

questions.question: State Health Index is an initiative of NITI Aayog, in collaboration with Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and with technical assistance from the ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Institute for Competitiveness**__.

questions.question:
Which of the following is a purpose of remote sensing satellites?

I. Draught assessment

II. Estimation of yield of various crops
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Remote sensing satellites** are used for various applications, including monitoring environmental conditions and agricultural practices.

• **Draught assessment:** Remote sensing technology is instrumental in identifying regions affected by drought. By analyzing satellite imagery, experts can monitor soil moisture, vegetation health, and water bodies to predict and manage drought conditions. *Hence, statement I is correct.*

• **Estimation of yield of various crops:** Satellites equipped with sensors can evaluate the health and productivity of crops. Data derived from remote sensing enables accurate estimation of crop yield by monitoring factors like chlorophyll content, crop growth stages, and land usage. *Hence, statement II is correct.*

• Both applications showcase the ability of remote sensing satellites to assist in agricultural management and environmental monitoring. *Thus, the correct answer is Both I and II.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Remote Sensing Satellites:**

• Remote sensing satellites are equipped with advanced sensors to capture data about Earth's surface from space.

• They utilize technologies such as optical imaging, infrared sensing, and radar to analyze land, water, and atmosphere.

• Examples include India’s **RISAT** (Radar Imaging Satellite) and the USA’s **Landsat** program.

• These satellites play a crucial role in monitoring natural disasters, urban planning, resource management, and environmental conservation.

• **Drought Monitoring:**

• Remote sensing identifies drought-prone regions by analyzing vegetation indices like **Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)**.

• It tracks water availability in reservoirs and rivers using radar and optical sensors.

• This technology aids in effective water resource management and disaster preparedness.

• **Crop Yield Estimation:**

• Satellites monitor agricultural fields to predict crop yield by analyzing factors like vegetation health and growth patterns.

• Techniques such as multispectral imaging help in assessing soil conditions and crop productivity.

• For example, India’s **Resourcesat** satellite provides critical data for agricultural planning.

• **Global Examples:**

• **NASA’s MODIS:** Used for global vegetation monitoring and drought analysis.

• **European Space Agency's Sentinel:** Provides high-resolution imagery for agricultural applications.

• **India’s Cartosat:** Offers detailed mapping data for environmental and agricultural use.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Key Benefits:**

• Remote sensing satellites provide real-time data, enabling proactive decision-making in agriculture and disaster management.

• They reduce dependency on ground surveys, saving time and resources.

• **Applications beyond agriculture:**

• Used in urban planning, forest management, and climate change studies.

• Critical for monitoring natural disasters like floods, earthquakes, and cyclones.

questions.question: The 'Mangalyaan' mission of India was launched by, which of the following launch vehicle?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**PSLV**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Mangalyaan**, officially known as the **Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM)**, is India's first interplanetary mission launched by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)**.

• The mission was launched on **5th November 2013** using the **Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV-C25)**, a reliable and cost-effective launch vehicle developed by ISRO.

• **PSLV**, or Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, is known for its versatility and has been used to launch satellites into various orbits, including geostationary, polar, and interplanetary orbits.

• The Mangalyaan mission's objective was to study the **Martian atmosphere, surface, and mineralogy**, and demonstrate India's capability in interplanetary space missions.

• The **PSLV-C25** successfully placed the Mars Orbiter into Earth's orbit, which later transitioned into a Martian orbit, marking India's entry into interplanetary exploration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV):** 

• PSLV is a medium-lift launch vehicle developed by ISRO and has been operational since its first successful flight in **1994**.

• It is known for its versatility and has launched satellites into polar, geostationary, and interplanetary orbits.

• PSLV is a four-stage rocket with alternating solid and liquid propulsion systems, making it highly reliable for diverse missions.

• It has been used for launching satellites like **Chandrayaan-1**, **Mangalyaan**, and various Earth observation satellites.

• **Mangalyaan Mission:** 

• India became the **first Asian country** to reach Martian orbit and the **first nation globally** to do so in its maiden attempt.

• The mission cost approximately **₹450 crore**, making it one of the most cost-effective Mars missions globally.

• Mangalyaan carries five scientific instruments to study **Martian surface features, morphology, atmospheric composition**, and dynamics.

• The mission's success established ISRO as a significant player in the field of space exploration and interplanetary missions.

• **Other ISRO Launch Vehicles:** 

• **SLV-3:** The Satellite Launch Vehicle-3 was India's first experimental satellite launcher, used in the early 1980s.

• **ASLV:** The Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle was developed in the late 1980s but had limited success.

• **GSLV:** The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle is used for heavier payloads and launches into geostationary orbits.

• Each of these launch vehicles contributed to the development of India's space program, but **PSLV** has been the most versatile and reliable for interplanetary missions like Mangalyaan.

• **Significance of Mangalyaan:** 

• The mission demonstrated **India's technological capabilities** in space exploration and interplanetary missions.

• It helped in the study of **Martian surface and atmosphere**, paving the way for future Mars exploration missions.

• Mangalyaan's success brought global recognition to ISRO and enhanced India's position in the international space community.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **PSLV Achievements:** 

• PSLV has completed over **50 successful launches**, including missions for foreign clients.

• It launched a record **104 satellites in a single mission** (PSLV-C37) in February 2017.

• **Global Impact:** 

• Mangalyaan established India as a space-faring nation capable of conducting cost-effective space missions.

• The success of Mangalyaan encouraged collaborations with other space agencies like **NASA, ESA**, and others.

• **Future Missions:** 

• ISRO is working on future missions like **Chandrayaan-3** and **Gaganyaan**, India's first human spaceflight program.

• Further Mars exploration missions are being planned based on the data gathered by Mangalyaan.

questions.question: The "Chandrayaan-2" mission was launched by, which of the following launching vehicle?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**GSLV**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chandrayaan-2**, India’s second lunar exploration mission, was launched on **July 22, 2019**, by the Indian Space Research Organisation (**ISRO**).
 
• The mission was launched using the **Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mark III (GSLV Mk III)**, also known as **“Bahubali”**.
 
• **GSLV Mk III** is a three-stage heavy-lift launch vehicle developed by ISRO, specifically designed to carry heavier payloads into higher orbits.
 
• The primary objective of the Chandrayaan-2 mission was to explore the **South Pole of the Moon**, which remains a relatively unexplored region.
 
• The GSLV Mk III successfully placed the **Chandrayaan-2 spacecraft** into a highly elliptical orbit around Earth from where it proceeded on its journey to the Moon.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV Mk III):**

 
 
• The **GSLV Mk III** is the heaviest and most powerful launch vehicle developed by ISRO, capable of carrying payloads of up to **4 tons** into Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO) and **10 tons** to Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
 
• This launch vehicle has three stages: a solid rocket booster (S200), a liquid core stage (L110), and a cryogenic upper stage (C25).
 
• The cryogenic stage (C25) uses **liquid hydrogen** and **liquid oxygen** as propellants, providing the necessary thrust for the final stage of the mission.
 
• The GSLV Mk III was also used for launching India’s first manned space mission, the **Gaganyaan** mission.
 
 
 
• **Chandrayaan-2 Mission:**
 
 
• **Chandrayaan-2** consisted of three components: an **Orbiter**, a **Lander (Vikram)**, and a **Rover (Pragyan)**.
 
• The mission aimed to study the Moon’s topography, mineralogy, exosphere, and the presence of water ice in the permanently shadowed regions near the poles.
 
• The **Vikram lander** attempted a soft landing on the Moon’s surface but lost communication during the final descent. However, the **Orbiter** continues to function and send valuable scientific data.
 
 
 
• **Other Launch Vehicles:**
 
 
• **SLV-3:** India’s first experimental satellite launch vehicle, capable of placing payloads in low Earth orbit. It was used for the **Rohini satellite** in 1980.
 
• **ASLV:** Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle was developed to improve payload capacity but was phased out due to limited capabilities.
 
• **PSLV:** Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle is known for its reliability and versatility in launching satellites into polar and geosynchronous orbits. It is primarily used for launching Earth observation satellites.
 
 
 
• **India’s Lunar Exploration Program:**
 
 
• The **Chandrayaan-1** mission, launched in **October 2008**, was India’s first lunar mission and confirmed the presence of water molecules on the Moon.
 
• **Chandrayaan-3**, a follow-up mission, aims to achieve a successful soft landing on the Moon and is in development.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **GSLV Mk III** is also known as **LVM-3** (Launch Vehicle Mark-3) and was developed indigenously by ISRO.
 
• The launch of **Chandrayaan-2** marked a significant milestone for India in the global space exploration community.
 
• The **South Pole** of the Moon is of great interest due to the potential presence of water ice and the possibility of future human exploration.
 
• India became the **fourth country** in the world to attempt a soft landing on the Moon, following the United States, the Soviet Union, and China.

questions.question: Which of the following factors determine the state of a substance whether it will be solid, liquid or gas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pressure and Temperature**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 __ 
• The **state of a substance** (solid, liquid, or gas) is primarily determined by its **pressure** and **temperature**. These two factors control the phase transitions between different states of matter. 
• **Temperature**: Higher temperatures provide particles with more kinetic energy, allowing them to overcome intermolecular forces and transition from solid to liquid (melting) or liquid to gas (evaporation). 
• **Pressure**: Increasing pressure forces particles closer together. At high pressures, gases can condense into liquids or even solids. Conversely, reducing pressure can allow substances to transition to gaseous states more easily. 
• For example, **water** exists as ice, liquid water, or steam depending on the specific combination of pressure and temperature. At standard atmospheric pressure, water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C. 
• Phase diagrams are used to represent the relationship between pressure, temperature, and the state of a substance. They show the conditions under which a substance exists as a solid, liquid, or gas. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Density and Viscosity:** These properties are characteristics of a substance and do not determine its state. For example, honey is highly viscous but is always in a liquid state under normal conditions. Similarly, density changes with the state but does not directly define the state of matter. 
• **Pressure and Density:** While density is influenced by pressure (e.g., compressing a gas increases its density), it is not the sole determinant of a substance’s state. Pressure and temperature together influence phase changes. 
• **Temperature and Weight:** Weight is a measure of gravitational force on a substance and has no relevance in determining its state. Temperature, however, is a critical factor in phase transitions. 
• **Phase Transitions:** Common phase transitions include melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), vaporization (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), sublimation (solid to gas), and deposition (gas to solid). 
• **Critical Point:** At the critical temperature and pressure, the distinction between liquid and gas disappears, and the substance exists as a supercritical fluid. This is a unique state of matter with properties of both gases and liquids. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Triple Point:** The triple point is the specific pressure and temperature at which all three states of a substance (solid, liquid, and gas) coexist in equilibrium. For water, this occurs at 0.01°C and 611.657 Pascals. 
• **Real-life Applications:** Understanding pressure and temperature is crucial in fields like meteorology, material science, and engineering. For example, refrigeration systems rely on controlling pressure and temperature to achieve desired cooling effects. 
• **Examples of Phase Changes:** Dry ice (solid CO2) sublimates directly into gas at atmospheric pressure, while metals like iron transition between solid and liquid phases during smelting processes. 
• **Phase Diagrams:** These graphical representations help visualize the conditions under which substances change states, aiding in industrial and scientific applications such as chemical synthesis and material design.

• **Sawai Jai Singh II**, the ruler of Amber (later Jaipur), was a renowned astronomer and mathematician who constructed **five astronomical observatories**, known as **Jantar Mantars**, in different parts of India.

• The observatories were established in the cities of **Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura, and Varanasi**.

• These observatories were built during the early 18th century, between **1724 and 1734**, under Sawai Jai Singh's supervision.

• The purpose of these observatories was to make **accurate astronomical measurements**, aid in the preparation of astrological charts, and improve the study of celestial movements.

• The most prominent of these observatories is the **Jantar Mantar in Jaipur**, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site and contains the world's largest stone sundial, known as the **Samrat Yantra**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Architectural Significance:**

• The observatories are known for their unique and innovative **architectural designs**, combining science and aesthetics.

• Each Jantar Mantar includes several instruments made of stone and brass, such as **sundials, astrolabes, and quadrants**, which were used for astronomical calculations.

• **Scientific Contributions:**

• Sawai Jai Singh II was inspired by **Islamic and European astronomical techniques**, such as those of Ptolemy and Ulugh Beg.

• He compiled the **Zij-i Muhammad Shahi**, an astronomical table based on observations from his observatories and earlier works.

• **Preservation of Observatories:**

• Most of the observatories have been preserved, with **Jaipur's Jantar Mantar** being the most well-maintained and popular among tourists.

• The Jantar Mantars are recognized as historical landmarks and represent India's rich scientific heritage.

• **Decline of Mathura Observatory:**

• The Jantar Mantar in Mathura has been lost due to neglect and urban development, leaving only four of the original five observatories intact.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **UNESCO Recognition:**

• The Jantar Mantar in Jaipur was designated as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **2010** for its cultural and scientific significance.

• **Legacy:**

• Sawai Jai Singh II's efforts in astronomy exemplify India's contributions to science and mathematics during the **Mughal period**.

</ul

questions.question: What tragic incident happened in the life of Robert Clive in 1774?

options.text: He was given death penalty on the charges of corruption

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**He committed suicide.**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Robert Clive**, also known as **Clive of India**, played a key role in establishing British control over India during the 18th century. However, his later life was marked by controversies and personal struggles. 
• In **1774**, Robert Clive died by **suicide**. He was found to have used a penknife to end his life at the age of **49**. 
• Clive suffered from **health issues**, including chronic pain due to gallstones, and was known to take opium for relief, which likely contributed to his mental health struggles. 
• His life was also marred by accusations of **corruption** and **mismanagement** during his tenure in India. He faced severe criticism in Britain after returning from India, which may have exacerbated his emotional and psychological distress. 
• While his achievements in India were significant, including the victory at the **Battle of Plassey (1757)**, his later years were overshadowed by personal and professional challenges. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Early Life and Career:** 
• Robert Clive was born in **1725** in England and joined the **British East India Company** as a clerk in **1744**. 
• He played a pivotal role in consolidating British power in India, especially with his victory at the **Battle of Plassey**, which marked the beginning of British dominance in Bengal. 
• **Controversies and Corruption:** 
• Clive faced accusations of **embezzlement** and misuse of power during his time in India. 
• He was summoned by the British Parliament in **1772** to defend his actions, and although he was ultimately exonerated, the scrutiny took a toll on his reputation and mental health. 
• **Health Issues:** 
• Clive struggled with **physical ailments**, including gallstones, and his dependence on opium for pain relief likely worsened his psychological state. 
• Mental health support and understanding during the 18th century were limited, leaving him vulnerable to emotional distress. 
• **Legacy:** 
• Despite his tragic end, Clive is remembered as a key architect of British imperialism in India, laying the foundation for nearly two centuries of British rule. 
• His contributions remain a subject of debate, with critics highlighting his role in exploiting India, while others focus on his military and administrative accomplishments. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Battle of Plassey (1757):** This battle marked the beginning of British control over Bengal and eventually much of India. Clive's victory over Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah was a turning point in Indian history. 
• **Dual Administration:** Clive introduced the system of dual administration in Bengal, where the British controlled revenue collection while the Nawab retained nominal authority. 
• **Parliamentary Inquiry:** Clive faced intense scrutiny in the British Parliament, leading to significant stress and a tarnished public image, despite his acquittal. 
• **Influence on British Imperialism:** Clive's policies and victories laid the groundwork for the expansion of British influence in India, making him a pivotal figure in colonial history. </ul

questions.question: In the context of the Indian Parliament, the ______ Reading refers to the discussion on the motion that the Bill or the Bill, as amended, be passed.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Third**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Third Reading** in the context of the **Indian Parliament** is the final stage of the legislative process where the Bill is discussed for its passage. 
• During this stage, the focus is on the motion that the Bill, either in its original or amended form, should be passed. No new amendments are introduced at this stage. 
• The discussion in the Third Reading is typically brief and revolves around the overall merits and implications of the proposed legislation. 
• Members of Parliament (MPs) vote on the Bill at the end of the Third Reading, and it is either passed or rejected. 
• If the Bill is passed by one House of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha), it is sent to the other House for consideration and approval. 
• The Third Reading ensures that the Bill aligns with its intended purpose and has undergone thorough scrutiny in the prior stages (First and Second Readings). 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **First Reading:** 
• This is the introductory stage where the Bill is formally introduced in either the Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha. 
• There is no detailed discussion on the Bill at this stage. The objective is to present the Bill and seek permission to proceed with it. 
• Once introduced, the Bill is published in the Gazette of India to inform the public and legislators. 
• **Second Reading:** 
• This stage involves a detailed examination of the Bill. The Second Reading is divided into two sub-stages: 
• General Discussion: Members discuss the principles and objectives of the Bill. 
• Clause-by-Clause Examination: Each provision of the Bill is reviewed, and amendments may be proposed and debated. 
• The Bill may also be referred to a Parliamentary Committee for further scrutiny during this stage. 
• **Voting Process:** 
• At the end of the Third Reading, members vote on the Bill. Voting can be conducted through voice vote, division vote, or electronic voting, depending on the circumstances. 
• If the Bill is approved in its current or amended form, it proceeds to the next legislative step, such as approval by the other House or assent by the President. 
• **Legislative Process in India:** 
• The legislative process in India follows a structured framework defined by the Constitution and parliamentary rules. 
• It includes various stages such as drafting, introduction, readings, voting, and presidential assent before a Bill becomes an Act. 
• This process ensures transparency, accountability, and inclusivity in lawmaking. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Role of the President:** 
• Once a Bill is passed by both Houses of Parliament, it is sent to the President for assent. 
• The President can approve the Bill, withhold assent, or return it for reconsideration (except in the case of Money Bills). 
• Once the President gives assent, the Bill becomes an Act and is enforceable as law. 
• **Money Bills and Third Reading:** 
• Money Bills, as defined under **Article 110** of the Constitution, deal with financial matters like taxation and public expenditure. 
• These Bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha, and the Third Reading ensures their alignment with national financial policies. 
• **Role of Parliamentary Committees:** 
• During the legislative process, Bills may be referred to Parliamentary Committees for in-depth examination and recommendations. 
• This ensures that laws are comprehensive, effective, and aligned with the needs of the people. </ul

questions.question: Which of the following enzyme is secreted by the pancreas for digesting emulsified fats in humans?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lipase**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
• **Lipase** is an enzyme secreted by the pancreas that plays a crucial role in the digestion of **emulsified fats** in humans. 
• Emulsified fats are broken down into smaller fat molecules by bile salts, which are produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder before lipase acts on them. 
• **Pancreatic lipase** specifically hydrolyzes triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids, making them absorbable by the small intestine. 
• Lipase is active in the **small intestine**, where it interacts with fat molecules and bile salts to facilitate digestion. 
• The secretion of lipase is stimulated by the presence of fats in the small intestine, and its activity is essential for fat metabolism and energy production. 
• **Bile salts**, although not enzymes, aid lipase in emulsifying fats and increasing the surface area for enzymatic action.

questions.question:
Which of the following waste product is stored in old xylem of plants?

I. Resins

II. Gums
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Old xylem**, also known as heartwood, serves as a storage site for waste products in plants.
 
• **Resins** are complex chemical substances secreted by plants, which are often stored in the old xylem. These substances help in sealing wounds and protecting the plant from pathogens. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• **Gums** are water-soluble substances produced by plants, usually as a response to injury or infection. They are also stored in the old xylem. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• Both resins and gums serve as defense mechanisms for plants, helping them deal with environmental stress and microbial attacks.

questions.question: In the context of the Sangam age of South India, the term "Sangam" refers to ______ .

options.text: a royal festival of Tamil kings
a gathering of South Indian traders
an assembly or "meeting together" of Tamil poets

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**an assembly or "meeting together" of Tamil poets**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The term **Sangam** refers to the gathering or assembly of Tamil poets during the **Sangam Age**, which is a historically significant period in South Indian history.
 
• The Sangam assemblies were held to compile, critique, and refine Tamil literature, showcasing the cultural and literary richness of the Tamil people.
 
• The Sangam Age is believed to span roughly from **300 BCE to 300 CE**, covering the early historic period of Tamilakam.
 
• These assemblies are said to have taken place under the patronage of the Tamil kings, primarily the **Cheras, Cholas, and Pandyas**, who supported poets and scholars.
 
• The Sangam literature includes works on various themes such as **love, war, ethics, and governance**, providing valuable insights into the socio-political and cultural aspects of the era.
